analysis.one_liner: Forces big-bank credit cards to run on at least two competing payment networks to lower swipe fees.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 9 House cosponsors from both parties, never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Large banks and the Visa and Mastercard networks currently lock most credit cards to their own processing systems and collect a fee on every swipe. This bill would require banks with more than $100 billion in assets to let merchants route credit transactions over at least two networks not affiliated with the issuer, including the two largest networks, and would bar banks from penalizing merchants for choosing a cheaper route. It also directs the Federal Reserve to publish a list of payment networks that pose a national security risk or are tied to foreign governments. Banks and card networks say the lost fee revenue funds credit card rewards; retailers say the savings would show up in lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants, from large retail chains to small businesses, would gain the ability to route credit card transactions to whichever network charges less, reducing the swipe fees (interchange) they pay on every sale. If merchants pass some of those savings on, consumers would benefit through prices. Smaller payment networks would gain access to transaction volume now reserved for Visa and Mastercard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants and payment networks outside the duopoly

how_it_helps.text: Banks with more than $100 billion in assets could no longer restrict a credit card to a single network or to networks they own or control; every card would have to be processable on at least two networks, and merchants could not be forced onto the two largest ones.
Card issuers could not penalize a merchant, financially or otherwise, for routing a transaction to a cheaper network, or for failing to send a set volume of transactions to a particular network.

The Federal Reserve, with Treasury, would have to publish and update a list of payment card networks that pose a national security risk or are owned, operated, or sponsored by a foreign state entity, and those networks could not be used.

analysis.who_pays: The largest credit card issuers (banks with over $100 billion in assets) and the Visa and Mastercard networks would lose the routing control and fee revenue they currently lock in. Banks warn that swipe fees fund rewards programs, so cardholders could see reduced points and perks if the bill passed.

drawbacks.text: Swipe fee revenue on credit cards funds the points and cash-back that cardholders receive; banks argued that cutting routing fees on the largest issuers would squeeze those rewards programs, and that because smaller banks are exempt from the bill, their cards would keep richer rewards while large-bank cards lose them, pushing customers away from community bank cards.

The bill does not touch the three-party model (cards where the issuer is also the network, such as American Express and Discover), so a large share of the market would be exempt, and savings would reach merchants directly only in the part of the market it covers; whether consumers see lower prices depends on merchants passing savings along, which the bill does not require.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, measurable cost — swipe fees that merchants pay on every credit transaction and generally recover through prices — and uses a straightforward mechanism already tested on debit cards after 2010. The honest costs are that cardholder rewards would likely shrink, that consumers benefit only if merchants pass savings through (which is not guaranteed), and that the $100 billion threshold and the three-party exemption leave big parts of the market untouched, protecting community banks and American Express and Discover while concentrating the hit on the largest issuers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lance Gooden (R-TX) introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 on June 7, 2023, with Reps. Lofgren, Tiffany, and Van Drew as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — is recorded in its history.
It ended the 118th Congress with 9 cosponsors (5 Democrats and 4 Republicans) and never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large credit card networks and the biggest bank issuers keep the current system, in which their networks handle most transactions and collect a fee on each one. Merchants and the smaller networks that would have competed for that volume gain nothing this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Lance Gooden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors (5 of 216 Democrats, 4 of 224 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

for.name: Merchant and retail trade groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for credit card routing competition, arguing merchants pay billions in swipe fees each year.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the committee's two years; the action record shows no committee activity after referral.

against.name: Large credit card networks and big-bank issuers
against.role: Visa, Mastercard, and major card-issuing banks
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against routing mandates, arguing the bill would cut interchange revenue that funds rewards and would effectively regulate only the largest banks.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but thin: 5 of 216 House Democrats and 4 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored, and the bill died in a Republican-held committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill bars issuers from restricting cards to the two largest networks or to affiliated ones, opening Visa and Mastercard's lock on transaction routing to competition. Their per-transaction fee revenue would fall if merchants could route to cheaper networks.

industries.industry: Large bank credit card issuers (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: These issuers collect interchange fees on every swipe and control which networks their cards run on; the bill takes away both. The revenue also funds the rewards programs their cardholders use, which is the banks' main objection.

Merchants pay swipe fees on every credit sale and pass much of that cost into prices; routing competition would let them choose cheaper networks. Small businesses would benefit alongside large chains, which is why retail trade groups backed the bill.

industries.industry: Smaller card-issuing banks and credit unions (under $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: They are exempt from the mandate, so their interchange revenue is untouched while large-bank competitors could face reduced rewards on their cards. Their gain comes from the bill carving them out rather than from anything consumers get.
Cards where the issuer is also the network are explicitly exempt, so the bill leaves their closed-loop business intact while weakening their two big rivals.
Networks other than the two largest would gain access to transaction volume on big-bank cards for the first time, which is the bill's core competition mechanism.
